title.en: Gii-Nitaa-Aadisooke, Ojibwe Legends from Lac Seul

div.title: Gii-Nitaa-Aadisooke, Ojibwe Legends from Lac Seul
div.speaker: Christie Ningewance

paragraph.text_eng: Once, a long time ago, there was a small family of Anishinaabe people living in the wilderness -- a man, his wife, and their two sons. Every day, that man would go into the forest to hunt for food, get firewood, and to do anything that would help them survive. And in the evening he would come home, bringing food.

sentence.sent_text: Endaso-giizhig awe inini ando-anokii noopimiing e-andwenjiged, e-manised, wegonen igo e-inanokiid.
Gii-onaagoshininig dash ako bi-giiwe, e-biidood miijim.

paragraph.text_eng: And that woman stayed at home looking after their home. But every day, that man would come home and he would find that their wiigiwaam was still dirty. There was no food being cooked. So he would have to cook. And the boys always looked dirty. He finally asked his older son what his wife did in the day-time while he was away.

sentence.sent_text: Awe dash wiin ikwe abi imaa endaawaad enaagajitood odaawiniwaa.
Endaso-giizhig dash gii-bi-giiwed awe inini odoonji-waabandaan giiyaabi wiininaagwanini owiigiwaam.
Gegapii o-gagwe-jimaan gaa-zaziikizinid ogozisan aaniin ezhichigenid owii-wan gii-ondendid gabe-giizhig.

paragraph.text_eng: “She always fixes herself up,” said the boy. “And then she goes away all day. She doesn’t come back until much later in the afternoon,” said the boy. The man didn’t say anything.

sentence.sent_text: Baamaa gii-ishk-waa-naawakwenig jibwaa-dagoshinan bi-giiwe," inaajimo gwiiwizens.

paragraph.text_eng: The next morning, the man went into the forest. But he did not go far. He only went as far as the treeline. He wanted to watch his wife. He saw her fixing herself up. She was combing her hair and putting on her good dress. And then she went into the forest. She left her children behind to look after them-selves.

sentence.sent_text: E-ani-waabaninig apane iinzan miinawaa gopii awe inini.
Gaawiin dash wiin geget waasa izhaasii.

paragraph.text_eng: He secretly followed the woman. He had to know where she went.

sentence.sent_text: O-giimooji-biminizhawaan owiiwan awe inini, e-wii-gikendang aaniindi ko ezhaanid.

paragraph.text_eng: That woman stopped at a large tree. She knocked on the tree. A woodpecker stuck his head out. That woodpecker came flying down immediately when he saw the woman. They lay down beside each other on the ground. So it was a woodpeck-er that she lay with all day. So the man found out what was going on. That man hid there. Not until later in the afternoon, the woodpecker and the woman got up from the ground. The woman went home. The woodpecker flew up the tree. It was that man’s turn to go to the tree. He knocked. He stood close by. Sure enough the woodpecker stuck his head out. He grabbed the woodpecker by the neck. He broke its neck. He plucked him and gutted him. Then he began walking home. He killed a partridge on his way home. He didn’t say anything when he got there.

sentence.sent_text: Zhemaak gii-bi-niisaandawebizo awe baapaase e-waabamaad ini ikwewan.
Baapaasen ngwana gabe-giizhig gaa-wiipemaad awe ikwe.
Baamaa wiikaa gii-ishkwaa-naawakwenig made-wanishkaawag awe ikwe gaye awe baapaase.
Wiinitam awe inini izhaa imaa mitigong.

paragraph.text_eng: When it was morning again, they all got up. The man start-ed to cook the morning meal. He cooked the woodpecker. He fed his wife. The woman gorged on the food. He spoke to his wife.
“Do you know who you are eating?” he said to her.
“I'm eating a partridge!” the woman said.

sentence.sent_text: "Bapashki gosha awe gaa-amwag," ikido awe ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: “You're eating your lover,” he said to her. “I killed that woodpecker you've been sleeping with.” The woman began crying loudly. Her crying angered her husband. He attacked her. After he had killed his wife, he threw her body into the fire. Then he began getting ready to leave. That woman’s body was burning in the fire. He spoke to his children. “I am leaving for good. Use these items to save yourselves from danger.” He gave them four items -- a small smooth rock, a comb, and two more items. And then he left.

sentence.sent_text: Omiinaa' niiwin gegoonan -- asiniins, binaak-waan , miinawaa niizhininiwan gaa-gii-miinaad.

paragraph.text_eng: And so those boys were left behind. They were crying. And then one boy began poking at the eye holes of the woman’s skull as it was laying in the fire. Finally it spoke to him, “It is you two who told on me. I would not have been killed.” The Skull suddenly rolled out of the fire as it was talking to them. The boys immediately began running away from it. The Skull began rolling and chasing them as they ran.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig dash awe gwiiwizens oboopoojaaba'aan iweni otigwaan-igegan gaa-ayaanig imaa ishkodeng.
Wenji-gidaaboodenig iweni otig-waanigegan imaa ishkodeng, bekish gaagiigidoomaganini.
Amii go zhemaak ezhi-biminizha'ogowaad iweni otigwaanigegan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so those boys ran in fear. They ran pretty quickly and covered a good distance. But that rolling Skull kept coming towards them. And as it rolled, it yelled out to them, “Rolling Skull is catching up to you! Rolling Skull is catching up to you!” They could see that Skull in the distance. The smaller child was beginning to tire from running. Then the older brother remem-bered that he had those items from his father. He used the Comb.

sentence.sent_text: Amii go gaye iwe otigwaanigegan ebiidaaboodenig.
Amii dash iinzan gaa-inwemagak iwe otigwaanigegan ebiibaagiimagak, "Ditibitigwaan gidadimigonaawaa, ditibitigwaan gidad-imigonaawaa!"
Amii dash awe gaa-zaziikizid gwiiwizens gaa-izhi-mikwen-dang ji-aabajitood bezhig iwe gaa-gii-miinigopan odeden.

paragraph.text_eng: “Would it be that there is a great tangled forest!” he yelled. And immediately there was a thick tangled forest that separat-ed them from the Skull. The Skull was deterred by the tangled brush for a long time. It got stuck now and again. That gave the boys ample time to rest so that they could begin running again. They ran for along time at their leisure.

sentence.sent_text: Apane debwe wiinge gichi-zagaakwaa imaa gaa-gii-izhi-webinang iweni binaakwaan.
Ginwesh wiin igo gwiiwizensag gaawiin o-gii-waabamaasi-waawaan.

paragraph.text_eng: After some time, they heard that voice calling to them, "Rolling Skull is catching up to you! Rolling Skull is catching up to you!” Sure enough, they could hear it cracking through the bushes, coming at a good pace. They ran harder. The little brother was crying in fear, and he was starting to get tired again. The older brother decided to use the second item his father had given him. He threw one of the helping tools behind him and yelled, “Would it be that there is a great swamp!”

sentence.sent_text: Aazha miinawaa ayekozi awe gwiiwizens bezhig.
Ishehay, aazha miinawaa o-debaabamaawaan e-biidaaboozonid Diti-bitigwaanan.
Amii dash noongom gaa-doodang awe gwii-wizens gaa-zaziikizid, e-gii-aabjiwebinang aabajichigan.

paragraph.text_eng: Sure enough, a huge swamp thick with moss and cattails appeared magically. That stopped the Skull in its tracks. It had to carefully manoeuvre the swamp so it would not sink into its morass. Again, this bought the boys some time to rest and sleep knowing that the Rolling Skull would not be able to catch up to them for a while. The next morning they began running again.

sentence.sent_text: Debwe miinawaa mashkiig miziwe imaa ayaamagan gaa-gii-on-jibatoowaad.
Mamaandaawanoon aaniish ini aabajichi-ganan gaa-gii-miinigopan odeden awe gwiiwizens.
Aapiji ginwesh miinawaa imaa gii-dazhi-gagwaadagitoo e-gagwe-gash-ki'od Ditibitigwaan.
Amii miinawaa gii-ani-gashkitoowaad ji-anweshinowaad igi gwiiwizensag, gaye ji-nibaawaad e-ayekoziwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Again, after some time, they heard a voice in the far distance, “Rolling Skull is catching up to you! Rolling Skull is catching up to you!” They ran as fast as they could but the voice was getting more distinct. “Rolling Skull is catching up to you! Rolling Skull is catching up to you!” So the older brother threw the third item behind them, yelling “Would it be that there is a great mountain range!” And sure enough there was an immense mountain range that appeared behind them. For sure, that mountainous range stopped the Rolling Skull for a long time.

sentence.sent_text: Noongom dash asiniinsan o-gii-aabajiwebinaan awe gwiiwizens.
Debwe dash wiinge gii-gichi-ayinaabikaa imaa gaa-gii-izhi-bangishing awe asiniins.
Amii sa miinawaa gii-aadaabikishing awe Ditibitigwaan.

paragraph.text_eng: The two boys rested again but kept running during the days. They were running for a long time when they heard the voice in the far distance again, “Rolling Skull is catching up to you! Rolling Skull is catching up to you!” Again, they ran faster until the smaller boy got too tired and cried. Now the older brother had only the last item left to help them. He threw it behind and he yelled, “Would it be that there is a River there between the Skull and us!” And sure enough, there was a huge river that separated them from the Rolling Skull.

sentence.sent_text: Amii miinawaa gii-gashkitoowaad ji-gichi-bimi-batoowaad igi gwiiwizensag e-gii-anwebiwaad gaye.
Amii dash ishkwaawaach michi-bezhigwanini ge-aabajitood awe gwiiwizens.
Odaabajiwebinaan iweni ishkwaawaach aabajichigan, amii dash ekidod, "Daa-gii-gichi-ziibiiwan omaa!"

paragraph.text_eng: That stopped the Rolling Skull in its tracks again. It rolled back and forth along the shore wondering what to do. Then it spotted a Swan swimming close by. It called out to the Swan, “Handsome Swan! Please take me across the river on your beautiful back! In return, I will be your lover!”

sentence.sent_text: Aana-aa'aazha-waaboozo iinzan imaa jiigew, e-wawaanendang aaniin ge-gii-onji-aazhawa'ang.
Daga aazhawa'oon-ishin agaaming, meshkwach dash gi-ga-wiidigemin."

paragraph.text_eng: “How can you be my lover when you have no body? You are just a Skull!”
“I have these eye holes in my skull where you can have your pleasure,” answered the Rolling Skull. It could never run out of answers.

sentence.sent_text: "Omaa nishkiinzhigong nindizhi-bapagonez, amii imaa," iinzan izhi-nakwetam awe Ditibitigwaan.

paragraph.text_eng: “I suppose so”, said the Swan, “but be careful not to hurt my back. Don’t move around once you're on my back. I’m very sensitive.”

“Alright,” said the Rolling Skull, and it rolled gently onto the Swan’s back. And the Swan began to swim across the great river, slowly. The Rolling Skull was getting impatient and began fidgeting and moving about on the Swan’s back.

sentence.sent_text: "Haaw," ikido Ditibitigwaan, wiinge minwendam ji-aazhawi'oonigod waabiziin.

paragraph.text_eng: “Keep still!” said the Swan but the Rolling Skull wouldn’t listen. It kept fidgeting and moving. It hurt the Swan and he moved to one side and the Rolling Skull slid into the water. So the Rolling Skull fell to the bottom of the deep dark river. And there it stayed. It could not move. And there it stayed forever. And from its eye holes, some tiny minnows came swimming out.

sentence.sent_text: Amii sa apane gii-bakobiised Ditibitigwaan, apane anaamiindim gii-izhise.
Amii dash imaa gaa-izhi-bagwaneshkiinzhigwed gaa-ondaad-agewaad aapiji gaa-agaashiinzhiwaad giigooyensag.

paragraph.text_eng: And so the two boys were sitting by the shore of the river, resting. They realized that they had survived the Rolling Skull. But the younger boy began crying again. His older brother didn’t know what to do. He decided to make a toy for him. When this special toy was tossed up in the air, it would make a musical sound. This amused the little boy for a long time.

sentence.sent_text: Amii awe gichi-gwiiwizens gaa-izhi-ozhitamawaad oshiimenzhan odaminwaagan.

paragraph.text_eng: During this time, they were unaware that someone was watching them. An old man had arrived in his canoe and was silently observing them. He willed it so that the toy would land inside his canoe. The older brother was surprised to see him. The old man put the toy on the end of his paddle and told him, “Come and get it.” The boy was reluctant but he had no choice. As he was reaching out for the toy, the old man suddenly shoved him into the canoe with his paddle and willed his canoe to speed away quickly. And they kept moving away, leaving his little brother behind. He heard his little brother crying loudly.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin dash nawaach gii-gikenjigesiiwag awiyan iinzan e-gii-odisigwaad, e-ganawaabamigowaad.
Imaa jiigew gii-jekogomo, jiimaaning namadabi awedi akiwenzi.

paragraph.text_eng: As they kept moving away further and further, suddenly he heard his little brother’s voice in his ear, his brother telling him, “Don’t worry about me, my brother. The Wolves have arrived and they’re going to look after me. I will be fine. They are show-ing me great love.”

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash ozaam waasa o-gii-ishpiwebinaan awe gwiiwizens iweni odaminwaagan.
Amii imaa biin-doonag gaa-izhiseg iwe odaminwaagan.
Odabwiing o-gii-niimaako'aan iwe odaminwaagan awe akiwenzi.

paragraph.text_eng: And so the older brother felt a big sense of relief that his younger brother would be looked after by the Wolf pack.

sentence.sent_text: Apii dash e-wii-odaap-inang , apane awe akiwenzi ezhi-biindoonewebawaad ini gwiiwizensan.
Amii sa gaa-izhi-na'endang awe gichi-gwiiwizens e-gikendang ji-mino-ayaanid oshiimenzhan.

paragraph.text_eng: So finally the old man brought the young boy to his desti-nation. Wemishoozh was the name of the old man. His two daughters met them as they were arriving. They saw that their father had brought home a young boy. They fought over who would have that young man for a husband. The older sister won the right to have him.

sentence.sent_text: Amii gegapii gii-bagamiwinigod ini akiwenziwan awe gwiiwizens.
Niizhiwag ikwewag imaa gaa-bi-naanzibiiwaad e-waabamaawaad odedewaan.
Mamaakandiwag igi ikwewag awenen ge-onaabemid ini gwiiwizensan.

paragraph.text_eng: That night, the young woman told the boy to put his head on her arm as they slept. “In the morning, you will be a man.” Sure enough when he awoke in the morning, he had become a full-grown man instead of a boy.

sentence.sent_text: Amii eni-dibikaninig, odigoon ini ikwewan oni-kaang ji-izhikweshing nibaad.

paragraph.text_eng: And so he married that woman. Eventually he had three children with his wife. He was content. He had no worries.
But one morning, his father-in-law spoke to him. He said to him, “We should go gathering seagull eggs. I know a place where there are a lot of seagull eggs.”

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash aabiding e-giizhigag oganoonigoon ozhishenzhan awe inini.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright,” said the young man. And so they went off. Now the old man was a very spiritually gifted person. He had a magic canoe. All he had to do was tap the canoe and it would move forward in any direction he wanted, just by the power of his thoughts.

sentence.sent_text: O-michi-bakite'aan ojiimaan amii dash eshkwaad ezhi-maajiishkaamagak iwe jiimaan.

paragraph.text_eng: There, they found many seagull eggs when they got to the island. The young man picked as many eggs that they would eat. After, he finished picking, he walked over to where he had left his father-in-law. He saw him riding away in his magic ca-noe. “Hey! You're leaving me behind!” he yelled at him but of course, that was the old man’s intention. So the young man stood there wondering what to do. The seagulls would be com-ing back soon and they would peck him to pieces if they found him there alone. Then he remembered that he once dreamed of a seagull when he was a child and the seagull had blessed him with his love.

sentence.sent_text: Apii gaa-ishkwaa-odaapinang minik ge-miijiwaad, apane wedi gakiiwe gaa-izhi-danenimaad ozhishenzhan.
Amii naanaagadawendam aaniin ge-izhi-chiged awe inini.
Amii go ji-nisigod gaachidinigod imaa ini giiyaashkwa'.
Amii dash gaa-inendang, nin-gii-zhawenimigoban itagiin gii-yaashk gii-abinoojiiwiyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Sure enough, a seagull landed. He killed it and he cut it open. He somehow entered the seagull’s body and flew up-wards. He was also able to take some seagull eggs with him. He flew upwards and towards his home. On his way home, he flew over Wemishoozh as the old man was riding his magic canoe home. Wemishoozh was laying down, facing the sky, snoozing. The young man defecated on his father-in-law and it landed on Wemishoozh’s forehead. “Yohoo!” was all Wemishoozh said. He thought it was a seagull doing that to him.

sentence.sent_text: Apane ezhi-miijinaad ozhishenzhan, mayaa oskatigong izhi-bangisinini omoow awe inini.

paragraph.text_eng: When the young man got home, he asked his wife to cook the eggs quickly. When they were cooked, he had his children eat them at the shore so their grandfather could see them when he arrived.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-dagoshing, oganoonaan owiiwan, "Wewiib giizizan ono waawanoon."
Gaa-ishkwaa-giizizang, o-gii-inaa' oniijaanisa, naanzibiing ji-dazhi-miijinid ini waawanoon, ji-waabamigowaad omishoomisiwaan dagoshininid.

paragraph.text_eng: Wemishoozh arrived at the shore in his canoe. He saw his grandchildren eating seagull eggs.
“And where did you get those seagull eggs you are eating?"
“Our father went seagull-egg hunting and brought them home to us,” his grandchildren said to him.
“How bountiful a life you have, having such a father!” is all he said to them. And he went up to his wiigiwaam. He didn’t say another word after that. His son-in-law beat him at that time.

sentence.sent_text: "Debiziyeg odedeyeg," iinzan eta gii-ikido awe akiwenzi.

paragraph.text_eng: Wemishoozh was laying on his back one day. He wasn’t saying anything. His grandchildren were playing happily outside. The old man was looking at something across the lake. His son-in-law spoke to him finally.

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding miinawaa egiizhigak, aazhigidaagoshin agwa-jiing awe Wemishoozh.
Wiinge wiinawaa ini oozhisa'jiikiba'idiwag imaa agwajiing.

paragraph.text_eng: “What are you looking at?” the younger man said to him.
“I’m watching the moose I see walking along the shore across the lake.”
“It’s just the head lice that are walking on your forehead that you see. You think you are seeing moose,” he said to the old man.

sentence.sent_text: "Gidikomag gosha igi gaa-babaamosewaad giska-tigong ," odinaan akiwenziwan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Hm!” is all the old man said.

chapter.eng_title: The Boy Who Was Taken By The Moon

paragraph.text_eng: Once upon a time, long ago, there was a boy who lived with his parents in the forest. This was the teaching long ago for young children, not to look at the moon for long periods.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding iinzan gwiiwizens ayindaaban noopimiing mewinzha, e-biboong.
Amii dash iinzan bizhishig gaa-izhi-onji'ind abinoojii gaawiikaa dibikigiizisoon ji-gichi-ganawaabamaad.

paragraph.text_eng: One evening, a young boy’s mother told him to go get a pail of water from the lake.

sentence.sent_text: O-gii-anoonigoon dash omaamaan aabiding ji-naa-da'ibiid e-onaagoshininig.

paragraph.text_eng: It was a beautiful clear night. The full moon was shining up above. It was fully round and the night was bitterly cold. So the boy went down to the lake holding his pail and his dipper. He went to his ice hole where they got their water from. He looked up at the sky and saw the round full moon. He couldn’t help himself and stared long and hard at the moon. It was at that moment that the moon took him. Suddenly he wasn’t vis-ible anymore at that ice hole. That boy was gone. Back at his home, they waited for him to return but he never came back. When they went to the ice hole, they found his tracks leading there but not returning. And that’s how they knew that the moon had taken him. And so now when you look up at the moon, you will see him standing up there, still holding his kettle and his dipper.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iinzan ezhi-naanzibiid awe gwiiwizens, odakonaan odakikwan gaye ogwaaba'igan.
Wedi dash gii-dagoshing dwaa'ibaaning, ishpiming iinzan gii-inaabi.
Amii sa eshkwaad gii-odaapinigod ini dibikigiizisoon.
Amii gaa-onji-gikendamowaad dibikigiizisoon iinzan e-gii-odaapinigod awe gwiiwizens.
Inashke dash inaabiyin gi-ga-waabamaa awe gwiiwizens dibkigiizisong gaa-made-niibawid ogwaaba'igan giiyaabi gaa-dakonang.

chapter.eng_title: The Boy Who Was Cared For By The Bear

paragraph.text_eng: Once, a long time ago, there was a boy who lived with his parents. One day they went into an area to pick blueberries, far away from their wiigiwaam. While they were there, the boy wandered off by himself away from where his parents were. Soon, he didn’t know where he was and he called for his parents and they didn’t answer his calls because he was so far away. He kept on going. Then he was certainly lost. He sat down and cried, knowing he wouldn't find his parents. Then he heard a voice. He looked and there was a big black bear looking at him. “Don’t cry, my grandchild,” said the bear. “I will look af-ter you.”

sentence.sent_text: Gii-gopiiwag dash aabiding eniibing e-wii-mawinzowaad waasa noop-imiing ezhi-miinikaag.
Waasa dash gii-bake'adoo imaa awe gwiiwiz-ens gaa-dazhi-mawinzonid oniigi'igoo'.
Ajina go gii-babaa-ma'adoo e-gagwe-mikang nawach ezhi-baatiinadaninigin miinan.
Biinish gii-wanishin, gaawiin ogikendanziin aaniindi mayaa gaa-gii-bi-ondosed.

paragraph.text_eng: And so the bear took him to her den that night. The next day, they went gathering blueberries. And this is how they spent the summer, eating blueberries and raspberries and any other berries that were edible and ripe. Each night when they went to their den, the bear would bend over these birchbark boxes and out of her mouth would come all the blueberries and raspberries she had eaten that day. They would be stored there, and they’d keep. That was the way of the bear. Some-times they ate fish. Except this was not cooked fish like he was used to. It was rotten fish that was riddled with maggots. The bear ate with relish. He couldn’t. Then the bear made it so that when he looked at the maggots, he saw cooked wild rice. That he could eat and he ate all that. Soon the summer came to an end and the bear started to get clumsy and sleepy as the days got colder. She began spending more time in the den. She spoke to the boy and explained that when winter came, she would sleep all winter. She would not wake up until the spring. You have these boxes of berries to eat all winter, and fish and wild rice. You will have enough to survive the winter. It will be cold but you can lay next to me and I will keep you warm. Stay close to me and you will be fine. You will not be lonely because I will be here all the time. I am just sleeping. Do not go out there or you will freeze to death. When the spring arrives, we will have made it through the winter. You will find your family.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gabe-niibin gaa-izhi-babaa-wiijiiwaad awe gwiiwizens ini makwan.
Endaso-giizhig iinzan ako gii-babaa-ningaapoonowag miinan gaye miskomina'.
Wegonen igo dinookaan miin gaa-miijing o-gii-miijinaawaa.
Amii iinzan ako ezhichiged awe makwa, enigok e-ningaapoonod gii-niibininig.

paragraph.text_eng: And so that winter, that’s what he did, He kept close to her and kept warm. He never felt lonely because he knew his bear grandmother was there with him, just sleeping, because that’s what bears do in the winter. Finally, it began to be warmer. And with the warmth, his grandmother began to move about and slowly wake up.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-giiwewaad dash ako imaa waazhing gaa-izhidaawaad, amii ezhi-animikotaad awe makwa.
Wiigwaasi-makakong dash ezhi-ziigisenigin gakina ini miinan gaa-gii-miijid gii-gichi-daawanid.
Amii ngwana edoondang emawinzod gewiin makwa.
Ngoding gaye naanew babaamaazhagaame-wag , giigoowan e-ando-gaachidinaawaad.
Ngoding gaye omikawaawaan bigishkani-giigoowan e-abinid imaa michi, mitaawangaang jiigibiig.

paragraph.text_eng: They were able to go outside and everything was begin-ning to turn green. There were fish to eat. That is when the bear told the boy that it was time for him to return to his own people. She had taught him something that he needed to learn. She told him which direction to walk, to find his family. She told him that he would grow up to be a fine hunter. She instructed him to always respect bears, never to hunt them and kill them for they were his relatives. And he went.

sentence.sent_text: Memindage dash ookwewaazonind ini giigoowan odizhi-minopwaan awe makwa.
"Ishke inaabin, noozhis," iinzan odigoon makwan aabiding.
E-ganawaabamaad dash ini giigoowan, gaawiin okwewaazosiiwan gii-izhinam.
Amii sa bizaanigo gewiin gaa-inanjiged awe gwiiwizens gabe-niibin.

paragraph.text_eng: He found his family after a few days. By now he was almost a young man. He grew up to be a fine man who was a great hunter. He raised his children and taught them what he had been taught by the bear. He never killed a bear. He taught oth-ers to respect the bear because the bears are our relatives. He grew to be a very old man.

sentence.sent_text: Ndigo gaye gii-ani-noondezi gii-babaama'adood awe makwa inendaagozi.
Gi-ga-giizhooshkawin gisinaag, amii omaa nimbiiwaying izhishinin giikajiyin.
Gaawiin gaye gi-ga-zhagadendanzii aaniish zhaagooch omaa nin-ga-ayaa.
Wiin wiin awe gwiiwizens miinan o-gii-miijinan gaa-gii-mawinzwaadang.
Amii imaa makwang gaa-izhi-ni-baanid gewiin gaa-izhi-ashijishing e-giizhooshing wiinge.
Amii dash iwe apii gii-bagidinigod ji-giiwed awe gwiiwizens ini makwan.
Amii gaa-igod gego wiikaa ji-gagwe-nisaasig makwan, bizhishig ji-mikwenimaad ini-wiiji-makwan gaa-gii-zhawen-imigod.
Ginwesh gii-bi-maadizi awe gwiiwizens, biinish gii-gichi-ininiiwi.
Gaawiin dash gaye wiikaa makwan o-gii-nooji'aasiin ji-gag-we-nisaad gaa-gii-ako-bimaadizid.

chapter.eng_title: Thunder Bird Women Marry the Human Men

paragraph.text_eng: Once upon a time, long ago, there were ten brothers living by themselves in the wilderness. They were quite content to live by themselves. There was no woman to care for them. Every-day, they went out to hunt for their food and in the evening, they would return to their camp and look after things there. They would clean their wiigiwaams and get water, firewood, and cook their evening meal. And then the next day, they would go off again. They lived like this every day.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinawaa eta imaa daawag, gaawiin wiin ikwewan owii-jidaamaasiwaawaan.

paragraph.text_eng: One day, they came home to their camp and found that someone had cleaned their camp, got water and the firewood. All they had to do was cook the food they brought home. They wondered how that had happened, who had come to do this for them. The next day, they went off again to hunt for their food all day long. In the late afternoon, they arrived home and again, all was clean in their camp and the water and firewood was there for them. It was a big mystery. Finally Majiikiwis, the oldest brother said that he would stay home the next morning and stay hidden and find out who was doing this for them.

sentence.sent_text: Majiikiwis gii-izhinikaazo awe maawach gaa-zaziikizid osayenzimaa.
Awe dash miinawaa gaa-ani-oshiimen-zhimaawid Majigaakaagiwaaz gii-izhinikaazo.
Awe dash maawach gaa-oshiimenzhimaawid Biipiigiwisenz gii-izhini-kaazo.
Gaawiin dash wiin wiikaa nin-gii-noondaziin aaniin gaa-izhinikaazowaagwen igi nisawiya'ii gaa-gii-ayaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: The next morning he stayed behind and hid. All day long, he stayed hidden and no one came. His brothers arrived in the late afternoon and the camp was as they had left it in the morning. There was no water and no firewood for them.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-onaa-goshininig dash ako bi-giiwewag imaa gaa-izhi-daawaad.
Naadinisewag, naada'ibiiwag, manisewag, daataashkiga'inisewag, bag-wa'igewag , jiibaakwewag, giziibiiginigewag, bekichigewag, ozhiitaawag miinawaa ani-waabaninig ge-aabajitoowaad.
Amii sa iwe gaa-doodamowaad enda-so-giizhig igi ininiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: The next day, the second oldest brother declared that he would stay home and see if he could find the person who had been doing this for them. Sure enough, that’s what he did. He stayed hidden, like his older brother. All day long, he stayed hid-den and no one came.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash e-onaagoshininig dagoshinoog igi ininiwag.
Wenji-waabandamowaad wiinge aazha awiyan e-gii-bekitamaagowaad endaawaad.
Aazha gaye gwayaanch imaa gii-atewan misan, gaye nibi.
E-ani-waabaninig apane miinawaa gabe-giizhig noopimiing gii-ondendiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: The third day, the third oldest brother said he would stay and try to find out the person who had been helping them. Again, it was the same result. No one came in the daytime. Each day, the next younger brother stayed to try to find out their benefactor. Finally on the last day, it was Biipiikiwisens, the youngest brother who said he would give it a try. His older brothers all laughed at him. How could he succeed when his more experienced and more accomplished brothers had failed? Still, he convinced them that he should be allowed to stay be-hind and find out who had been helping them in their camp.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-bigiiwewaad aazha miinawaa wiinge bekichigaad-eni gaa-izhidaawaad.
Wiinge sa go maamakaadendamoog awegwenan imaa gaa-biizhaanigwen gii-ondendiwaad.
Amii dash eta ge-onji-gikendamang awenen ako omaa gaa-biizhaad."

paragraph.text_eng: That morning, he sat hidden in his wiigiwaam. Not too long after his brothers had left, he heard the sound of wings flut-tering in the sky. He sat there. Then he heard the footsteps of someone walking about on the ground. Again he heard the flut-tering wings over and over. Finally, he had to look. He peered outside his wiigiwaam and he saw a beautiful woman with long wings tidying up the camp. She flew to the lake with empty pots and filled them with water and flew back to the camp. She flew to the bush and got firewood for the campfire. She did all this while flying. When she was done, she stood there at the centre, and waited for him to come out of his wiigiwaam. He did so. Their eyes met and he was drawn to her. He walked over and they began talking to each other. He felt like he had known her for along time. He didn’t want to stop talking to her, nor to stop being in her company. He was happy. She smiled at him and he knew that she felt the same. They wanted to be with each other only.

In the late afternoon, his older brothers arrived and they were extremely surprised to find this beautiful woman with long wings at their camp, and their younger brother besotted with her. They saw that she would be their sister-in-law and treated her with that respect.

sentence.sent_text: Apii gii-bi-dagoshinowaad igi ininiwag, gii-onaagoshininig, gii-yaabi gii-wiinadanini endaawaad.
"Gaawiin gii-biizhaasii awegwen ako gaa-biizhaad," eta gii-ikido Majiikiwis.
Amii dash noongom Majigaakaagiwaaz wiin nitam gii-ikido ji-abid.

paragraph.text_eng: So their lifestyle changed when she began living with them. She looked after the camp while they went hunting every day. They were quite happy with this change. The brothers were happy for their little brother. All of them except for Majiikiwis. He was secretly smouldering in jealousy. He felt, why, why, why should the youngest brother get a beautiful woman for a wife? Why not him, as he was the oldest of them all, therefore, the best of them all? That was when he hatched a plan to get rid of his sister-in-law.

sentence.sent_text: Amii wiin nitam gii-gaazo imaa gabe-giizhig.

paragraph.text_eng: One morning, all the men got ready to go into the forest again. Only Majiikiwis lingered behind. He turned back to the camp, unknown to the rest. He ran to the camp. He saw his sister-in-law there by herself. He took an arrow from his quiver and shot her in the back. “Oh no! Why have you done this to me?” she cried. She was bleeding profusely from the wound. She immediately took to the sky. Majiikiwis turned around and went in the directions where his brothers had gone.
That evening, the men returned to the camp. It looked very messy. And their sister-in-law was nowhere to be seen. Right away they had a sense that Majiikiwis had something to do with this.

sentence.sent_text: E-ani-waabang, miinawaa awe gaa-ani-oshiimen-zhimaawid inini gii-abi.
Amii biinish wiin eta ishkose Biipiigiwis-ens.

paragraph.text_eng: “What did you do?” They asked him.

“Nothing,” he said. But they knew that he was lying. Then Biipiigiiwisens saw blood on the ground and some more drops of blood hanging in the air, all leading upwards. He burst into tears knowing that something had happened to his wife. He quickly got his traveling things together. He was going to follow her. And he was able to walk up into the sky, by following the drops of blood and the heart of his beloved wife.

sentence.sent_text: Nin-goding igo imaa gii-namadabid wenji-noondang ndigo miigwana' gaa-bidikwe'aangeshinonid e-initang.

paragraph.text_eng: When he reached the land of the clouds, he came to a small wiigiwaam. He looked inside and saw a small old woman sitting there by herself. She spoke to him when he entered. “Oh my grandson, there are spirits where you are trying to go. There is much hardship in store for you. But I will give you some tools to help you along the way.” So she gave him an enormous bird talon to use when climbing mountain cliffs, when he reached the land of the Thunder Birds.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash imaa gaa-izhi-ayaad awe ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: When he travelled the next day, he came to a huge moun-tain. He had no choice but to start climbing. Sometimes the mountain presented a steep cliff he had to climb. That’s when he used the talon given to him by the old woman. With it, he was able to climb up slowly. Slowly the talon began to be dulled by the hard rock. He managed to reach the top of the moun-tain. When he got there, to the land of the Thunder Birds, he couldn’t see any plants, not like on this earth. Everywhere he looked, he saw just rock. And he saw pools of red liquid that was not water. It was blood. He saw snakes laying in those pools. That was the food of the Thunder Birds.

sentence.sent_text: Apii dash gaa-dagoshinowaad igi ininiwag, aapiji o-gii-goshkowaabamaan ini ikwewan.
Endaso-giizhig ako gii-maajaawag gakina igi ininiwag.
Awe dash ikwe wiin gii-abi, e-bamitood iweni daawin.
Wiinge gii-minwendamoog igi ininiwag e-bami'indwaa weweni.

paragraph.text_eng: Finally he arrived at the village of the Thunder Birds. The Chief Thunder Bird met him at the gate and asked him why he had dared to come when his daughter had nearly got killed when she was with him. “I would like to see my wife,” he told the Chief Thunder Bird. “This is why I have travelled this far, why I have travelled this difficult road.”

sentence.sent_text: Amii iinzan gaa-inendang wiin e-zaziikizid wiin nitam ji-gii-wiidigepan.
Gaawiin wiin maawach gaa-oshiimenzhimaawid ji-gii-wiidiged nitam.
Amii iinzan gaa-inendang gegoon e-wii-doodawaad ini owi-inimoon.

paragraph.text_eng: Sure enough, he saw his wife. She had already begun to heal from the wound that her brother-in-law had inflicted on her. They were so happy to see each other. So the man was permitted to stay there with them.

sentence.sent_text: E-ani-waabaninig gakina igi ininiwag apane miinawaa gopiiwag.
Apane imaa opikwanaang o-gii-inawaan ini ikwewan.
Apane iinzan zhemaak ishpiming izhise e-bazigo'od, e-ozhimod awe ikwe.
Apane wiin gii-gopii Majiikiwis gii-ishkwaa-bimwaad owiinimoon.

paragraph.text_eng: It was very unsettling for him to live among the Thunder Birds, because of the cultural differences between them and the humans.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin gaye ngoji naagozisii awe ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: Each afternoon, the Thunder Birds would arrive in their village bringing what food they had killed. Biipiigiwisens was not very enthusiastic about eating the food they brought. They brought only snakes to eat. He was repelled by them. He grew rather thin after a while. Then a healer Thunder Bird made something for him so that he would believe that he was eating moosemeat and rabbits and so forth when they were serving snake flesh. In this way, he survived.
They also gave him the power to fly like them. That gave him parity, so he could kill his own food. He didn’t have to be fed by them.

sentence.sent_text: Zhemaak Biipiigiwisens owaabandaan miskwi ishpiming e-ani-agoodenig.
Amii go zhemaak gii-ozhi-itaabani'od e-wii-biminizhawaad owiiwan.
Amii gewiin ishpiming gii-ani-dadaakokiid gaa-izhikawenid ini binesiik-wen.

paragraph.text_eng: He lived with them for quite a while. Eventually, even though he was content to be there, he began to miss his broth-ers. He wondered how they were doing. He wanted to see them. He spoke to his wife one day, “I would be happy if we could go back to my home down below for a short while so I can see my brothers,” he said to her. His wife was kind-hearted and agreed to take him back for a visit.

sentence.sent_text: "Ishe, wiinge gosha zanagan wedi gaa-wii-izhaayin," odigoon.
"Gi-ga-miinin wiin igo ge-aabajitooyin ji-gashki'oyin ji-dagoshinan wedi."
Amii gaa-izhi-miinigod oshkazhiin ge-aabaji'aad ji-ak-waandawed aasamaabik, binesiiwaki ji-oditang.

paragraph.text_eng: So one day, they came flying back and flew for a long dis-tance. Finally they reached the land of the humans. He saw their wiigiwaams standing where he had last seen them but he didn’t see any sign of life. No smoke coming out of the chim-ney. There was no movement outside. I wonder where they went, he thought. He looked inside one wiigiwaam. He saw figures of people laying under dirt and dust. He poked at one of them.

sentence.sent_text: Amii gaa-izhi-aabaji'aad ini oshkazhiin gaa-gii-miinigod ini mindimooyen.
Zhaagooch gii-ani-gashki'o wedi waasa ishpiming gaa-izhi-dazhiikenid binesiwa'.
Apii wedi gii-dagoshing, gaawiin ngoji owaaban-danziin gegoon ji-nitaawigininig, daabishkoo wiin omaa akiing gaa-izhinaagwak.

paragraph.text_eng: “It’s me, Biipiigiwisens, I’ve come home,” he said. That fig-ure on the ground came to life and its arm shot a fistful of dirt at him, causing him to be blinded momentarily.

sentence.sent_text: O-gagwejimigoon aaniin gaa-onji-gagwe-biizhaad gegaa dash e-gii-nisimind odaanisan.
Amii iinzan ini odaanisan gaa-gii-wiidigemaad Biipiigiwisens.

paragraph.text_eng: “Go away from here, you dirty dog! You’re always lying to us, getting our hopes up!” said the man under the dirt and dust.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-bagidinaa iinzan awe inini imaa ji-ayaad maanoo.

paragraph.text_eng: “It’s true, it’s me, your youngest brother,” said Biipiigiwis-ens. And again he got another handful of sand thrown at him. It took a while before he was able to convince one brother that it really was him. That man made a big effort to open his eyes because his eyes were encrusted with dust. That’s how hope-lessly depressed he had become at losing his youngest brother. It had been such a long time since he had taken to his bed. One by one, all the men got up to see their little brother who was now a fine young man, and their sister-in-law. They didn’t say anything to Majiikiwis. He was also happy to see his little broth-er return. And so Biipiigiwisens and his wife stayed there with them for some time.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge dash iinzan gii-mayagendam wiinge aaniish bakaan izhitwaawag binesiwag, apiich giinawind gii-anishi-naabewiying.

paragraph.text_eng: Soon, one day, the woman spoke to her husband, “I guess we should think about getting back to my land.”

sentence.sent_text: Endaso-giizhig gii-onaagoshininig gii-dagoshinoog igi Binesiwag ebagamiwidoowaad gaa-gii-nitoowaad miijim.
Wiinge iinzan ako gaawiin owiinaapagendaziin Biipiigi-wisens ji-miijid gaa-miijinid ini Binesiwa'.
Ginebigoo' iinzan eta bizhishig gaa-bigiiwewinaawaad ji-amwaawaad.
Wiinge dash wiin ako awe inini gagwaanisagendam iwe ji-inanjiged.
Gegapii gegoon o-gii-doodawaawaan ini anishinaaben igi binesiwag, bizaanigo ji-gashkitood ji-mii-jid gewiin iwe gaa-miijiwaad wiinawaa, daabishkoo dash moonzo-wiiyaasing ji-izhinang ginebigo-wiiyaas.
Amii sa gabeya'ii imaa gaa-dazhiiked binesiiwakiing Biipiigiwisens.
Amii gewiin gaa-izhi-babaa-andawenjiged endaso-giizhig e-gii-biidamaazod ge-miijid.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright,” said Biipiigiwisens immediately to his wife. He loved her very much and didn’t want her to feel lonely for her own people. They got ready to leave the next day. That’s when Majiikiwis had the idea that he would like to go with them to the Thunder Bird country. Of course, they told him he could go with them. The woman wrapped her brother-in-law in a blan-ket. They told him, “We're going to wrap you in this but you must not poke a hole in it to try to look outside. You will fall out if you do that.”

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish aazha ginwesh imaa ayaa binesiiwakiing.
Odoonji-ganoo-naan owiiwan, "Nin-daa-minwendam ajina giiwey-ing , ando-waabamangwaa nisayenzag," ikido.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh, I wouldn’t do anything like that,” said Majiikiwis. And so they wrapped him in a blanket and tied it up good.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge gaye gaawiin awiya namechigesii imaa agwajiing.

paragraph.text_eng: They had lectured him for a long time on how to behave once they reach the Thunder Bird Country. They told him how to behave so he wouldn’t insult anyone. And he was also a very fussy person, that Majiikiwis. He was always very demanding. He was just a big bothersome person, to say the least.

sentence.sent_text: Apane ezhi-bim-waawaanga'ogod imaa gaa-bimishininid mitakamig, ebiz-ini'igod.

paragraph.text_eng: And so they flew off. After all Biipiigiwisens was able to fly like a Thunder Bird. And so they were flying through the sky, for a long time. Soon Majiikiwis was beginning to feel cloistered inside the blanket. He was getting bored. “I wonder what it looks like, where we're flying,” he thought to himself. “I don’t think anything much would happen if I just made a tiny little hole in this blanket.” He poked a tiny hole in the blanket. With that, it ripped wide open and he went falling out. He was tum-bling through the sky and his brother and sister-in-law were barely able to catch him and hang on to him until they got to their destination. That’s just the way he was. Whatever he was told not to do, that’s what he did.

They arrived at the woman’s village and they were greeted cordially by the Chief Thunder Bird who was happy to see his daughter come home again, safely. He didn’t know that this man was the one who had nearly killed his daughter. He treated him with courtesy and kindness because he was the brother of his son-in-law. And so Majiikiwis lived among the Thunder Birds. They saw that he was very different from his brother but they tolerated his shortcomings. After all, he was their guest and guests are always treated very well.

sentence.sent_text: Gegapii baamaa wiikaa o-gii-ani-debwetaagoon bezhig osayenzan.

Agaawaa o-gii-gashkitoon awe inini ji-doos-kaabid , aaniish wiinge ngwana gagiibwaawangaabi, gaa-apiichi-zaabendazig ji-wanishkaad imaa ishkwaawaach gaa-gii-izhi-gawishimopan, e-gii-gichi-mookawaanaa-pan iinzan oshiimenzhan.
Bepezhig gakina igi ininiwag ani-wanishkaawag, daabishkoo egoshkoziwaad gegapii.
Wiinge sa ozaami-jiikendamoog ewaabamaawaad oshii-menzhiwaan owiinimowaan gaye.
Amii sa imaa ajina gaa-ayaawaad Biipiigiwisens dago ini owiiwan.

paragraph.text_eng: The Chief Thunderbird had ten daughters. He decided that he would give his youngest sister for Majiikiwis to marry. She was very willing and Majiikiwi was very happy. He was fitting into the life there.

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding dash igo awe ikwe oganoonaan onaabeman.

paragraph.text_eng: One day, the two men thought they should try to go home. And the woman thought that she could invite her other sisters to come to the land of humans, and perhaps they would marry the brothers. And sure enough that is what happened. They all came down to their old camp and marriage ceremonies were performed and the humans made this great bond with the Thunder Birds.

sentence.sent_text: Ozhawenimaan aaniish owiiwan, gaawiin onandaweni-maasiin ji-zhagandendamonid.
Amii dash gaa-inendang Majiikiwis gewiin ji-izhaad binesiiwakiing.
Awe dash ikwe o-gii-gashkiiginaan owiinimoon waaboowaaning.
Amii gaa-inaad ini, "Amii omaa ge-izhi-gashkiiginigooyin, gego wiin gagwe-bagwanebidooken owe ji-gagwe-zaagidaabiyin.
Apane maajiisewag, aaniish gewiin Biipiigiwisens o-gashkitoon ji-bimised daabishkoo binesiing ani-izhiiyaa.
Wiinge sa maajii-gashkendamendam Majiikiwis imaa egashkiiginind.
"Gaawiin maawiin gegoon aapiji daa-izhises-inoon giishpin bangii eta bagwanebidoowaan owe," inen-dam.
Amii ndawaa gaa-izhi-minjiminaawaad baamaa wedi gii-dagoshinowaad e-gii-bagidinaawaad.
Amii naa bizhishig gaa-inaadizid awe Majiikiwis.
Wiinge sa naa o-gii-gichi-gaganoonaawaan Majiiki-wisan apii gaa-dagoshinowaad wedi.
Zhaangachiwa' ngwana oshiimenzha e-ikwewinid awe binesiikwe.
Maawach dash gaa-oshiimenzhimaawinid gii-miinaa Majiikiwis ji-wiiwid.
Ngoding dash igo, gii-inendamoog igi ininiwag, ji-gag-we-giiwewaad gaa-onjiiwaad.
Amii gaa-inendang awe ikwe ji-wiizhaamaad gakina oshiimenzha anishinaabewakiing ji-izhaawaad, ji-ando-wiidigemaawaad ini ininiwa'.

paragraph.text_eng: This did not happen a very long time ago. This happened in more recent times when people lived in log cabins. There was a family living in the forest, a man, his wife and son. They always taught their son how to live properly. They always talked to him, teaching him.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin wiin igo wiinge mewinzha owe gaa-gii-izhiseg-wen.
Apane iinzan o-gii-gikino'amawaawaan ogozisiwaan aaniin ge-ayizhiinid, bizhishig e-gii-waawiindamawaawaad gegoonini.

paragraph.text_eng: One of the things they taught him was to respect everything. They taught him to try to seek help from the world around him, because everything on this earth has a spirit.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iinzan ako gaa-izhi-gikino'amawaawaad onii-jaanisiwaan ji-manaajitoonid gakina gegoon.
Gaye ji-gag-we-andooshkang ge-wiiji'igod giishpin megwaashkang gaa-manidoowinig gegoon noopimiing, ji-ando-bawaajiged, ji-onji-miinigod manidoon ge-ani-aabajitood apii ani-gichi-ayaawid.
Gaawiin dash wiin gaye ji-onji-gagwe-gichi-wenoodizid ji-gagwe-izhichiged, maagizhaa gaye awiyan ji-gagwe-majidoodawaad.
Gaawiin wiin iwe o-daa-gagwe-ondinanziin ji-gikendang, gii-inaa.

paragraph.text_eng: They taught him to seek through his dreams, so that he would recognize it when spirit animals came to him that way. And he would be assisted by them when he became an adult. In adult life, he would always encounter a difficult life because that’s how it is. Every bit of help he got would help him later. He was taught not to seek financial wealth for himself, nor to wish any-one else any bad thoughts. He was taught not to seek that kind of help for himself.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash e-gizhebaawaganinig e-wanishkaawaad, wenji-noondang awe gwiiwizens gegoon e-gichi-madweyaakosenig agwa-jiing.
Amii iinzan ako gaa-igopan omaamaan, giishpin noondang gegoon gaa-maamakaazitang, ji-gagwe-waabamaad ini gaa-doodaminid, maagizhaa manidoowinid.
Obiizikawaagan dash jiigishkwaandem e-agoodenigiban o-gii-manibidoon e-bimi-zaagijibatood.
Apane maajiibatoo miinawaa, wedi gaa-danitang apatoo.

paragraph.text_eng: And so one very cold winter morning as they were getting up, the boy heard a very loud cracking noise outside. He ran outside right away. They were living in a log cabin. He ran over to where he thought the cracking noise had come from. His mother had told him that if he ever heard a strange cracking noise like that, he should go and see who was making that noise. That was the reason he had come running out. He had not had time to dress warmly. He just slipped into his winter boots. And he had grabbed his winter coat as it was hanging by the door. He didn’t see anything when he was outside. He stood still. Then he heard the sound again, and it was towards the treeline. He ran towards the trees where he heard the noise. He was running again. The snow was deep where he was running. He was getting cold but he kept on going. All he could think about was seeing who was making that noise.

sentence.sent_text: Aazha miinawaa wedi nawach waasa noopimiing madwe-noondaagwanini daabish-koo e-gichi-madweyaakwadininig gegoon initam.
Amii eta enendang e-wii-waabamaad ini gaa-noondawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Soon, he was far into the forest. His hands were now so cold that they were stinging. He had not brought mitts nor a hat. He stood in the middle of the snow amongst the trees. He wanted to give up and turn back. He had run far already and he was tired. Then he heard that noise again. I guess I’ll just keep going, he thought to himself as he ran again.

And then he arrived at a tall tree. He fell at the foot of the tree. He had trouble getting up from the snow, he was that cold. He looked up. He saw a tiny man sitting on the branch of the tree. The man was looking at him. He had never seen such a small person as that. The man was wearing clothing made out of smoked leather-—a jacket and leg coverings. Everything he wore was made out of leather. He was holding a bow and ar-rows. And he was holding something in his hand: a small mirror. He showed the boy the mirror. When he looked in the mirror, he could see an aerial view of the land around him. He could see rivers. He saw a moose walking along a river. That was a magic mirror this man was showing him. The man smiled at him. He spoke to the boy.

sentence.sent_text: Moonzwegin onji-ozhi-chigaadeni gaa-gigishkang biizikawaaganens, odaasan gaye.

paragraph.text_eng: “You are doing the right thing finding me. No matter how cold you were getting, you did not give up. That is the only way you will achieve things, if you don’t give up. That is what will help you when you become an adult. You will be able to kill moose, ducks, rabbit, anything you want to go after. I am Little Wild Man. I look after hunting. I will help you become a good hunter. Every time you go into the forest, I will be there to help you with your hunting. I will help you because you came look-ing for me with all your heart on this day.” And then that little man disappeared. The boy stood there by himself. He went home then. He was filled with awe at having encountered a mystical person.

sentence.sent_text: Amii aaniish eta ge-onji-gashkitooyin gegoon bagijiisiwan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so, it is told, that when he became an adult, the boy became a renowned hunter. Anytime he went into the forest to go hunting, he always came home with food to feed his family. That was because the Little Wild Man had blessed him with his good luck.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gaa-ikidonaaniwang, apii gii-gichi-ininii-wid awe gwiiwizens, aapiji iinzan gii-nitaa-andawenjige.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago, things were very different back then, not like today. There were spirits everywhere, there were creatures that existed that don’t exist now. Life was very difficult. There was much to be afraid of.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding iinzan mewinzha aapiji bakaan gii-izhiwe-ban.

paragraph.text_eng: A woman was living in the forest at this time. She had a husband. But she was not married to an ordinary human being. She was married to a giant penis. sentence.sent_text: Gaaw-iin dash wiin igo anishinaaben gii-onaabemisii.

paragraph.text_eng: It was also very cruel to her. Everywhere they went, she had to pull it along on a large sled. Even in the cold weather, she had to haul her husband.

sentence.sent_text: Miziwe gii-bimi-ayaawaad , odaabaanaakong ako o-gii-michi-bimidaabaanaan ini onaabeman.

paragraph.text_eng: Then one day, she could not live like that anymore.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash gegapii gii-inendam awe ikwe ozaam e-gichi-gagwaadagi'igod onaabeman.

paragraph.text_eng: She killed her husband. She hit it hard with an axe. She chopped up her husband into pieces. Then she scattered the small pieces in the snow. Those pieces of the penis spread out through the snow and magically small penises sprang up from the snow. They were the size of what is now normal size.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash imaa gooning gaa-izhi-webinang ini gaa-gii-bigishkada'ang.
Apane iinzan gaa-ispwaagonesegin ini gaa-gii-izhi-webinang imaa, niibiwa iinzan wiinagensan gii-onji-zaagikwebani'oomaganoon imaa gooning.
Daabish-koo noongom gaa-inigokwaagin wiinagan iinzan gii-inigok-waawan ini wiinagan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so she had said at that time, “From now on, this will be the size of that thing. In the future, it will never again be so big that it bullies human beings.” And so that is why today, the pe-nis is the size that it is. Some are bigger than others, and some smaller but they are never giant like that first one.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iinzan gaa-ikidogobanen awe ikwe, "Amii ge-inigokwaagin noongom ini dinookaanan ani-akiiwang!
Gaawiin miinawaa wiikaa da-gagwaadagi'iwemagazinoon iwe dinookaan."
Amii dash noongom bebakaan gaa-on-ji-inogokwaagin ini, aaninda agaasijiiyaawan, aaninda gaye mangijiiyaawan, e-ginwaakokin gaye aaninda.

paragraph.text_eng: One time, a very long time ago, Wiisakejaak was walking along ona frozen lake. Suddenly he heard voices in the distance, coming towards him. It looked like a pack of wolves. He heard them yelling to him, “Bad dog, Wiisakejaak, we’re going to eat you up when we catch you!”

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding igo onoondawaa' awiya' ebiidaadagaako-ba'idinid , ndigo ma'iinganag odizhinawaa'.
Onoondawaa' ebiibaaginid, "Maji-anim, Wiisakejaak, amii ji-amogooyin gaachidinigooyin!"

paragraph.text_eng: Wiisakejaak began running in the opposite direction. He was running for his life. Then he heard them laughing.

“We're just teasing you. We're not going to eat you, Wiisakejaak.” So he stopped, as he was quite out of breath an-yway. The wolves were very amused with themselves because they had made him run like the wind, for nothing.

sentence.sent_text: Amii gaa-izhi-gibichiid Wiisakejaak, aaniish wiinge akwa-naandam.
Wiinge gichi-wawiiyadendamoog igi ma'iinganag e-gii-dagakaanimi'aawaad Wiisakejaakwan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so they sat around visiting out in the middle of the frozen lake. The wolves said to him, “You know, we should have you join our pack for the winter. It’s a hard life eking a living in this cold weather.”

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gaa-igod ini ma'iingana' gii-nanaamadabi-waad mishawakom e-mawadisidiwaad, "Daga Wiisakejaak, gi-daa-gii-waawiijiiwishinaam noongom gaa-biboong.
Nawach da-wendan waawiiji'idiying apiich wiin baabezhi-goying.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright,” he said to the wolves. He liked the idea of trav-eling with the pack of wolves for the winter. It was difficult to secure his own food in the cold winter. So he was assigned one wolf to be his younger brother. And yes, eventually he and the young wolf began to see each other as close brothers.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig dash ini ma'iin-ganan gii-inaa ji-wiijiiwaad daabishkoo oshiimenzhan ji-inenimaad.
Debwe dash wiinge gii-ani-zaagi'idiwag igi Wiisakejaak awe dash ma'iingan.

paragraph.text_eng: All winter they travelled together. It was hard to get a moose. There were few moose that winter. And the snow was high. At one time, they were wondering what to eat next.

One night as they were getting ready to sleep for the night, he was given a wooden stick. It was kind of a rotten old stick. The leader of the wolf pack told him, “Put this under your pil-low when you sleep. Don’t look at it in the night to see what it looks like. Look at it in the morning. You will find a piece of moose intestine in its place in the morning.”

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge go biigijiisagan iwe mitig gaa-miinind Wiisakejaak.
Amii dash gaa-igod ini ogimaa-ma'iinganan, "apikeweshi-mon owe mitig nibaayin.
Gego wiin dibikag babaamendan-gen , ji-gagwe-waabandaman aaniin ezhinaagwak.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright,” said Wiisakejaak. “That can’t possibly happen,” he thought to himself.
“What did you say, Wiisakejaak?” said the wolf.
“I didn’t say anything,” said Wiisakejaak.
“That can’t possibly happen, is what you said, Wiisakejaak,” the wolf said to him. Wiisakejaak didn’t say or think anything after that.

sentence.sent_text: "Gaawiin editawe daa-izhisesinoon, gosha gidikid," Wiisakejaak," odigoon ma'iinganan.

paragraph.text_eng: So they all went to sleep. Wiisakejaak had that stick under his pillow. All the wolves were sleeping soon. Only Wiisakejaak found it hard to fall asleep. He was hungry. He was thinking about that stick under his pillow. “I wonder if it’s true what that wolf said?” he thought. So he felt under his pillow and sure enough, there was a piece of moose intestine. He took a big bite out of it. “They won’t know that I ate a little bit of this,” he thought. And he went to sleep.

In the morning, all the wolves were getting up and looking under their pillows and fining moose meat and other delicacies. Wiisakejaak looked under his pillow too and found only the old rotten stick which had a big bite out of it.

sentence.sent_text: Wiin eta Wiisakejaak gaawiin ogashkitoosiin ji-nibaad.
Gaawiin nin-ga-gikenimigoosii owe e-gii-miijiyaan bangii," inendam.

paragraph.text_eng: “What did you do, Wiisakejaak?” asked the wolf. “Did you secretly have a bite of it in the night?”

sentence.sent_text: E-wanishkaawaad dash igi ma'iinganag e-ani-waabang, gakina odoonjibidoonaawaan moonzonagizhiin gaye moonzowiiyaas imaa gaa-gii-izhikweshinowaad igi ma'iin-ganag.
Biigijiisag eta odoonjibidoon imaa, aabiding iinzan gaa-bakiinjigaadeg iwe biigijiisag.

paragraph.text_eng: “I didn’t touch it,” said Wiisakejaak. He sat there watching the wolves eat their breakfast. Finally someone took pity on him and fed him a bit of food. And Wiisakejaak thought to him-self, “What a tiny bit of food he gives me, that old dog”
“What did you say, Wiisakejaak?” said the wolf leader to him.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iinzan enendang Wiisakejaak e-ashamind wiiyaas, "Epiichi-bangii ashamid awe animoshish."

paragraph.text_eng: “I didn’t say anything,” said Wiisakejaak.
“What a tiny bit of food that old dog gives me, is what you said.” Again, Wiisakejaak had nothing to say after this. He knew he’d be heard every time he thought anything.

Then one morning, Wiisakejaak woke from a terrible dream. He dreamed of his younger brother wolf. So he told him his dream right away. He said to him, “Every time you reach a corner in your path when you're running or hunting, always toss a small stick in front of you. Never forget to do that, even if you are just about to get hold of a deer when you’re hunting. You will come to your demise if you don’t do it.” That’s what he told his younger brother wolf.

sentence.sent_text: "Epiichi-bangii ashamid awe animoshish gosha gidikid," ikido awe ma'iingan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so that is what the young wolf did every day when he was out running or hunting. He would stop and toss a small stick in front of him as he went around a corner. But one day, he was chasing a deer and he was catching up to it and just as he was about to get it, it veered to the side. He had no time to stop and throw a twig in front. The deer would have escaped. As soon as he went around the corner, he fell over a steep cliff with fast-moving rapids at the bottom. He fell to his death, the younger wolf brother of Wiisakejaak.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash miinawaa egizhebaawagag, gii-zegin-goshi Wiisakejaak.
Amii dash gaa-izhi-wiindamawaad zhemaak aaniin gaa-inaabandang.
Amii gaa-inaad, "Dasing gaa-oditaman e-waaninamok miikana gii-andawenjigeyin, bizhishig niigaan apagidoon mitigoons.
Gego wiikaa waniikeken iwe ji-doodaman, aanawi gegaa ji-debibinad waawaashkeshi andawenjigeyin.
Gi-ga-baataa'idiz giishpin iwe doodanziwan," o-gii-inaan oshiimenzhan.

paragraph.text_eng: Wiisakejaak sat there grieving for his younger brother. He told the rest of the pack what had happened. From there on, Wiisakejaak travelled by himself. It was now spring time and better to travel alone.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash debwe gaa-doodang bizhishig awe ma'iingan endaso-giizhig, gii-oditang ako gii-waaninibatood omiika-naang e-gii-niigaaniwebinang ako mitigoons.
Aabiding dash gegaa o-bimi-debamaan waawaashkeshiwan, waaniniba-toowan dash ini waawaashkeshiwan.

paragraph.text_eng: He had it in his mind that he wanted to kill whoever had killed his younger brother. He knew who they were and where to find them. The first thing he did was make a very large raft. He cut down big tall trees to get the logs. Then he tied them together to make this very strong raft. That was the first thing he did.

sentence.sent_text: Amii sa apane gaa-izhi-niisaabikised, waasa anaam-ing wedi gii-bimijiwanini ziibi.
Amii imaa nibiing gaa-izhi-bakobiised, waasa dash e-gii-ondagoojing.

paragraph.text_eng: Then he went to a river. He found a place that had fine sand on the shore of the river. He saw a kingfisher perched on a tree branch. He spoke to the bird.

sentence.sent_text: O-gii-wiin-damawaa' dash godag ma'iingana' aaniin gaa-izhisenid owiijiiwaaganan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Do you ever see the ones who own this river?” At first the kingfisher didn’t say anything. He was afraid to say anything. So Wiisakejaak promised to give him a beautiful scarf that he would wear forever. He was able to convince the bird to tell him what he wanted.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gaa-inendang Wiisakejaak e-wii-gagwe-nisaad ini gaa-gii-nisaanid oshiimenzhan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Yes,” said the kingfisher. “Every day when the sun is high in the sky, two big Water Cougars come out of the water. Then they lay down on the sand and sleep there. Then in the evening, they go back into the river. If you want to kill those Water Cou-gars, you must shoot their shadows with your bow and arrows. That’s the only way you'll be able to kill them.” So he was given these instructions how to kill the Water Cougars.

sentence.sent_text: Debwe imaa gaa-izhi-bimiji-wang ziibi wiinge minodaawangaa.

paragraph.text_eng: So he gave the bird the scarf. And today, that’s why the kingfisher has that crest on his head, that’s the scarf he was given to wear forever.

sentence.sent_text: "Wiikaa na giwaabamaag omaa gaa-dibendamowaad oweni nibi?"
Nitam gaawiin gegoon wii-ikidosii awe giishkimanisii.
Amii dash Wiisakejaak gaa-izhi-ashodamawaad ji-miinaad naabikaaganan ge-nepiji-gigish-kawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: And so he found himself an old hollow tree to stand be-side the river. And that’s where Wiisakejaak placed himself, inside the tree. He had his bow and arrow with him. And so he stood inside there. Soon, as it was high noon, he saw the Wa-ter Cougars come out of the river. They came slithering out of the river smoothly. My, they were looking very terrifying. They came walking towards where Wiisakejaak was. One was black and the other was white. They shook the water off their backs. Then they lay down on the sand. They made as if they were go-ing to sleep. But one of the Water Cougars spoke.

sentence.sent_text: "Endaso-giizhig gii-ishpi-giizhigag niizhiwag igi Mishibizhiwag gaa-ag-waaziiwaad omaa.
Giishpin dash wii-gagwe-nisadwaa igi Mishibizhiwag, gegoo wiin mayaa gagwe-miikawaaken imaa gaa-izhi-waabamadwaa.
Gaawiin wiin gi-ga-miz-hwaasiig , Imaa gaa-izhi-nichigidaawangishinowaad izhi-bimo.
Amii eta ge-izhi-nisadwaa," o-gii-igoon ini giish-kimanisiin.
O-gii-waawiindamaagoon igo aaniin ge-doo-dang ji-gagwe-nisaad ini Mishibizhiwa'.

paragraph.text_eng: “I don’t think that hollow tree was there before. I mean that one.” He came walking over to the hollow tree. He tried to pull it off the ground but Wiisakejaak stood firmly. The Wa-ter Cougar almost overpowered him but he managed to stay standing. “I wonder if Wiisakejaak is up to something?” said the Water Cougar. “No, maybe not.” And so they lay down and went to sleep.

sentence.sent_text: Amii gii-yaabi noongom ini gaa-gigishkawaad giishkimanisii okwe-ganing gaa-onji-izhinaagozid.

paragraph.text_eng: Wiisakejaak stood there for a long time to make sure they were fast asleep. And that’s when he stealthily came out of the tree with his bow and arrow. He aimed for the shadow of the black Water Cougar and shot. He heard it give a little sigh as it died. And then to the White one. Again that one made a little sigh as it died.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash debwe wiimbanakwadong gaa-izhi-bada-kinaad imaa jiigew.
Debwe e-ishpi-giizhiganinig, owaabamaa' eniizhinid Mishibizhiwa' e-made-moosh-kamonid imaa ziibiing.
Amii dash imaa ezhi-ag-waaziinid besho imaa gaa-izhi-gaazod Wiisakejaak.

paragraph.text_eng: And so that’s what happened with those Water Cougars. After they were shot and killed, a great amount of water came out of their bodies. It kept flowing and flowing.

Soon it was flooding the land. And that’s when Wiisake-jaak ran to the big raft and got on. He knew that other animals would be seeking refuge on that raft. Soon, all the different kinds of animals came running as the earth was being flooded with water. Rabbits, bears, snakes, bugs, ravens, any living crea-ture on this earth came crawling onto the raft.

sentence.sent_text: Baamaa wiinge gaa-gichi-nibaawaad gii-inen-dang , amii apii gaa-izhi-zaagidinaad omitigwaabiiman.
Gaa-izhi-nichigidaawangishinonid eta o-gii-izhi-bimwaan ini Mishibizhiwan, daabishkoo sa gaa-gii-izhi-wiindamaa-god ini giishkimanisiin.

paragraph.text_eng: And so they floated around on this raft for a long, long time. They looked out on the water every day. But they couldn’t see any land as far as they could see.

sentence.sent_text: Amii bezhigwan awe gaa-izhisenid e-gii-aanzanaamosenid gii-nibonid.

paragraph.text_eng: One day, Wiisakejaak thought he would ask the beaver to dive and look for earth underwater. He tied a rope on his foot so that if the beaver drowned, they would pull him back. So the beaver dove under the water. Wiisakejaak let the rope go. The rope was being pulled for a while until there was no movement at all. He pulled the rope and brought up the drowned beaver. He breathed the breath of life into him and the beaver came to life again.

sentence.sent_text: Amii ngwana ge-izhisewaad igi Mishibizhiwag, gaa-ishkwaa-bimondwaa, wiinge niibiwa nibi gii-onjiji-wanini imaa owiiyawiwaang.

paragraph.text_eng: This time, the Otter wanted to go underwater. Same thing, the Otter was gone under for a long time before the rope wasn’t moving anymore. He dragged up the drowned Otter, and breathed life back into him again.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash imaa obasooni-kaaning gaa-apatood Wiisakejaak.
O-gii-gikendaan imaa ji-bi-apa'iwenid imaa aya'aawisha', awensiwa'.
Debwe gakina gaa-daswewaanagiziwaad aya'aawishag awensiwag, gii-biijiba'iwewag imaa e-bimi-nikibiig aki.

paragraph.text_eng: “Let it be my turn,” said the Muskrat. The animals laughed at him because he was so small. Why would he be able to succeed when larger animals couldn’t succeed? But he was allowed to go down. He was the smallest. He was down under-water for a long, long time before the rope stopped moving. Then Wiisakejaak pulled up the drowned Muskrat. He too was drowned, like the other animals but he had something held inside his paw. When Wiisakejaak looked, he saw a clump of earth. He blew life into the Muskrat and he blew at the clump of earth too. Each time he blew, it would get larger. He blew and blew until he had created a large island.
And that is how Wiisakejaak had helped everyone survive the Great Flood.

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding dash Wiisakejaak o-gii-gagwejimaan amik-wan ji-googiinid, ji-gagwe-mikaminid akiini anaamiindim.
Ozidaang imaa gii-dakobizo zhinoodaagan awe amik, maa-gizhaa nisaabaawed, ji-michi-wiikwaabiiginaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: But the earth was not big yet. So he told the beaver to go around and drag his fat on top of the water. The beaver did that but he took the fat to where there were twigs and branch-es sticking out. That’s when the fat broke into smaller pieces and they floated everywhere.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge aaniish gewiin Nigig ginwesh nitaa-babaamaadage anaamiindim.

paragraph.text_eng: And the different animals came swimming over to help themselves to the fat. The bear took a lot of it which he smeared all over himself. That’s why the bear is fat. sentence.sent_text: Wegonen wiin ge-onji-gashkitoonid ji-bigiiwewidood akiini epiichi-agaas-hiinzhid wiin.

paragraph.text_eng: And so Wiisakejaak went walking along that shore. As he was walking, he heard a voice coming from the distance. He saw a huge frog hopping towards him. That giant frog was hop-ping towards him. She was crying bitterly.
“What are you doing? Why are you hopping around, and crying?” he asked the frog. And the frog answered him.

sentence.sent_text: O-gii-anoonaan dash amikwan ji-babaama'oodoonid obimidem Waiisake-jaak.
Ozaam dash gaa-izhi-mitigokaanig o-gii-ina'oodoon awe amik.
Amii miziwe imaa nibiing gaa-izhi-babaamaa'ang iwe bimide.

paragraph.text_eng: “Wiisakejaak has killed my grandchildren. That’s why I am crying. I am trying to heal them. That’s why I’m making those noises.” So Wiisakejaak hit the frog hard on the head and killed her. He cut her open and he crawled into her body and he went hopping away, and crying hard at the same time.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash imaa gii-madaabiiwaad aya'aawishag, awensiwag, e-wiii-odaapinamowaad gewiinawaa bangii iweni bimide.
Makwa wiinge niibiwa o-gii-zhizhoo'aan bimide wiiyawing.

paragraph.text_eng: He reached a village over there. When he arrived hopping, he saw a madogaan standing there. He went inside. He saw two dead Water Cougars laying on a rack inside the madogaan. He recognized them. Those were the same ones he had killed. He saw people sitting inside the madogaan. He asked them all to leave the madogaan, to go home. “This is the only way I will be able to heal my grandchildren,” he told them. And when he was alone in there, Wiisakejaak stabbed the two Water Cougars over and over. Then he quickly got out of the frog skin and ran off fast. He heard the people yelling behind him, “Oh no! It’s Wiisakejaak!” But by that time, he was already running far way. And that’s how he killed the Water Cougars who had taken his brother wolf’s life.

sentence.sent_text: Gewiin iinzan imaa waabooz o-gii-gagwe-zhizhoo'aan bimide wiiyawensing.

Amii gaa-izhi-bakonaad, gaa-izhi-biin-jishkawaad dash ini omagakiiwayaanan.

chapter.eng_title: When Wiisakejaak Posed as a Woman

paragraph.text_eng: Another time, Wiisakejaak was walking along a shore in the summer time. He had a hankering to eat ducks but he didn’t have a means of killing them. He saw a flock of ducks and loons and other water fowl not too far. I wish I could eat some of them, Wiisakejaak thought to himself.

chapter.eng_title: When Snapping Turtle Went to War

paragraph.text_eng: One time, Mikinaak the Snapping Turtle wanted to go fight a war. He felt like fighting a war. And so he decided that he must gather an army of warriors to go to battle with.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gaa-inendang ji-gagwe-maawadoo-naad ini ge-wiijiiwigod ji-andobaniid.

paragraph.text_eng: He went to the top of a hill and yelled, “Who will come with me when I go to battle? Who will go with me when I go to battle?” And so right away some young men came running.

“So show me how you will fight in battle,” he told them. And so the young men began making motions as if they were fighting, very intensely. “Ah no,” said Mikinaak, “You would be killed soon the way you’re moving. Sorry.”

“So how will you move around when you're in battle?” he asked the Raven. And the Raven showed him his moves. He flew up, and then he moved sideways and then he swooped down. He was very impressive. But he didn’t impress Mikinaak.

paragraph.text_eng: “It’s true what you say,” said Mikinaak. “I shall pick you to be in my army when I go to battle.”

paragraph.text_eng: And so that’s what happened to the turtles when they went to war. Mikinaak survived. He didn’t withdraw his head at all and so he was able to fight. And so the Anishinaabeg had a great feast of Turtle meat from that time.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago, there were Anishinaabeg living in the wil-derness somewhere. They lived near a lake. Things were very different back then than they are now. There was much to be feared all the time. People never knew what was going to come to their little village.

paragraph.text_eng: And one time, some people arrived in their vicinity. These were not like people as we know them. These were beings that were very large and were covered in hair. They called them Hairy Hearts. They arrived yelling, that’s how they announced their frightening arrival. paragraph.text_eng: Only one boy survived out of that group of people living in the village. He was orphaned when his parents were killed by the creatures. sentence.sent_text: Gii-mamaandaawizi maawiin igo gaye gaa-gii-onji-zhaabwiid awe gwiiwizens.

paragraph.text_eng: He made one attack at the Hairy Hearts. He killed one by the ice hole. He pushed him under the ice. Then he killed an-other. He used an awl to kill it. sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin wiin mookomaan, waagaakwad, bagamaagan gaye o-gii-ayaasiin.

paragraph.text_eng: He hid in the bush. He would spy on them. They couldn’t see him because he was well-hidden all the time. And he didn’t faint when he looked at them.

paragraph.text_eng: And so Jakaabes went up into the bush in the evening to go set a snare. He went over to where he had seen that big path. That path was so wide and trodden with many footprints. He set his snare there. And then he went home.

paragraph.text_eng: Then it was night time. Jakaabes went to bed. He slept all night. It was a very long night. The young woman got up finally. It was still dark. Then Jakaabes started moving around. He had lain in bed too long too.

paragraph.text_eng: They waited for morning to happen but it wasn’t hap-pening. It was still dark. “It’s such a long night,” said the young woman to her little brother. And the birds were not making any sounds at all, like they would normally in the early dawn.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin nawaach gaye gikendaagozisiiwag bineshiin-zhag wiiba ko gii-biidaabang gaa-noondaagoziwaad ako.

paragraph.text_eng: Then she saw a faint flash coming from the forest. Then it was dark again. That’s what kept happening. A big flash of light would appear and then darkness. Finally she spoke to her little brother, “What did you do yesterday?”

paragraph.text_eng: “It’s the Sun who got caught in a snare,” said the young woman to her little brother. What could they do to cut the Sun from his snare? When they tried to go near the Sun, they would get burned, because the Sun is so hot. One by one, the animals all tried to free the Sun from his snare. But they were deterred by the great heat. Finally it was the tiniest of creatures, the field mouse who was able to go near the Sun and bite the snare and set him free. And the Sun floated to the sky where he was able to walk across the sky once more.

sentence.sent_text: "Giizis ngwana awe gaa-gii-nagwaanad," odinaan ozhii-menzhan awe ikwe.
Aana-gii-naanzikawaawaad, amii ezhi-jaagizowaad, aaniish naa wiinge gizhizo giizis.
Gegapii maawach gaa-jiiboshkizhiid waabigozhiish waabiganoojii o-gii-gashkitoon e-naanzikawaad giizisoon e-gii-bakamaad.
Amii sa gii-gashki'od giizis, apane ish-piming gii-izhise.

paragraph.text_eng: Another time, Jakaabes spoke to his big sister, “My big Sister, please make me a new bow.” And so she made another bow for her little brother because she loved him so.

sentence.sent_text: Amii debwe gaa-izhi-ozhitamawaad mitigwaabiin, Ozhaweni-maan aaniish wiinge oshiimenzhan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Don’t shoot any arrows into the water,” she told her brother, “or the Sturgeon will swallow you up and take you.”

sentence.sent_text: "Gego wiin nibiing izhi-bimojigeken, gi-ga-googamig name," eta o-gii-inaan oshiimenzhan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright, my big sister,” he said to her. And so of course, he would do exactly what he was told not to do. He went walking off. He was eager to use his brand new bow.

sentence.sent_text: Apane iinzan gii-anima'adoo Jaakabes, wiinge jiikendam e-omitig-waabiimid.

paragraph.text_eng: He reached the great lake. Right away he aimed for the middle of the great lake and he shot his arrow there. He could see his arrow floating on the water. He took off his little jacket and he began swimming towards the middle of the lake. And while he was swimming along, he was singing this line, “I dare the big Sturgeon to swallow me up”. And sure enough a big Sturgeon came along and swallowed Jakaabes.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iinzan aanjigo bemi-ina'amaazod e-bimaadaged Jakaabes, "maanoo goog-amishin Name!"

paragraph.text_eng: And so, back at the camp, the sister was wondering where her little brother was. She quickly set a net. And sure enough, that very same Sturgeon was caught in that net. She cut open that Sturgeon.

sentence.sent_text: Wiiba go omedasinaan oshiimenzhan awe ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: She heard her little brother saying, “Be careful, my Big Sister, don’t cut me!” And that’s where she found her little brother, inside that great Sturgeon’s stomach. He was still alive. So she took him home right away.

paragraph.text_eng: Another time, Jakaabes was walking along the shore. He saw some beavers swimming about. He started bothering them, teasing them. He was pestering them. And so he finally got them angry and they came swimming towards his home. He hurried home. He asked his sister, “My older sister, where is my spoon?”

“Here’s your spoon,” his sister gave him his spoon which was a tiny clam shell. He quickly placed it down on the ground. Immediately they were inside a great big clam shell. It was very well shut off from the outside, no door, no opening at the top. He could hear people arriving outside.

sentence.sent_text: O-miinigoon odemikwaanan, esan iinzan ako odaabaji'aan gii-wiisinid Jakaabes.

paragraph.text_eng: “What did you do again, Jakaabes?” asked his sister.
“Nothing,” said Jakaabes. “I saw some beavers down the shore.” Those beavers sounded pretty angry outside the shell.
“This is where Jakaabes’s wiigiwaam was. It couldn’t pos-sibly be under that big rock. Let’s give up.” And those beavers went walking away again. They gave up trying to find Jakaabes.

sentence.sent_text: Amii apane miinawaa gii-animwewidamowaad igi amikwag.

paragraph.text_eng: Then one day, Jakaabes asked his sister, “What happened to our parents?”
