chapter.eng_title: The Vain Young Woman Who Married Moowas

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago, there were Anishinaabeg living in a village. In one family there was a man and wife and their daughter. The young woman was extremely beautiful and she knew it. Her parents had wished her to be married but she rebuffed all her suitors. The parents were at their wits’ end. She was a good worker. She could cook and sew and do all the things that young women do. Her only fault was that she rejected all the local men’s offers of marriage.

sentence.sent_text: O-daa-na-gagwe-wiidige'aawaan iinzan ako, bizhishig dash ako odaanawenimaan ininiwan aana-gagwe-wiidige'ind.
Aanawi sa wiin wiinge nitaa-anokii, amii dash eta odooke-aanawenimaa' ini ininiwa' gaa-gag-we-wiidigemigod.

paragraph.text_eng: Then one fall day, that young woman went into the forest to go and defecate after a meal. After she had done that, she stood there looking at her excrement, admiring it as it had different colours. And she spoke to it, “You are so beautiful! If only you were a man, I’d marry you.” And with those words, she went home.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash iinzan e-dagwaagig aazha, gii-gopii awe oshkiniigikwe, e-ando-miiziid noopimiing.

paragraph.text_eng: And so they lived there for that fall. One day just before winter, a stranger arrived in the village. No one knew him or where he came from. But his clothing was exquisitely embroi-dered and beaded. His moccasins, his mitts, his hat, his jacket were all beaded and decorated ornately. He was also very handsome to look at.

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding dash iwe e-biboong, wenji-dagoshing biiwide.
Awegwen awe, gaaw-iin ogikenimaasiwaawaan, dibi gaa-bi-onjiigwen.
Omakizinan, ominjikaawana', odaanikwaan, obiizikawaagan, wiinge mino-mamazinigwaadeniwan.

paragraph.text_eng: That is who the young woman decided to have as her husband. Sure enough, he was interested in her too. After they married, they settled beside her parents. They were quite hap-py. And the parents were pleased with their very pleasant new son-in-law.

sentence.sent_text: Amii sa gii-inenimaad awe ikwe ji-gii-wiijiiwaad ini ininiwan.

paragraph.text_eng: So now finally, the young woman had married. She was happy every day. And her husband was very loving towards her.

sentence.sent_text: Amii sa gegapii gii-wiidiged awe ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: Soon, the days started to get longer as it was evident that spring was coming. It was getting warmer. The man started to get restless, always looking out to the horizon. She panicked. She began packing her own things too. Her hus-band was walking away into the bush. She was filled with great sadness. She ran out too and began following him. But she couldn’t catch up to him because he had left much sooner, and walked faster.

She walked and walked, following his footprints. She was on snowshoes, following her husband. One day she found his mitt. “How careless he is,” she thought, and she slipped her hand inside the mitt. She took it out quickly because there was excrement in the mitt. “How totally careless he is, he doesn’t wipe himself properly,” she said, laughing.

sentence.sent_text: Amii gaawiin o-gii-adimaasiin, ozaam niigaan gii-maajaawan.

paragraph.text_eng: And she went walking again. Soon she found the other mitt. This was the other mitt. Again, she slipped it on and again, there was excrement on her hand. Again, she laughed and thought he was careless and sloppy in his habits.

sentence.sent_text: Ngoding igo wenji-mikawaad minjikaawanan iinzan gaa-baninaad awe inini.
"Epiichi-naa ganawendanzig odaya'iiman," iinzan eta ikido awe ikwe, apane ezhi-biinjiwebishkawaad ini minji-kaawanan.

paragraph.text_eng: It was a beautiful day the next day, now that it was spring time. The clouds were now white and fluffy in the sky. She was happy to be out and walking. And she was sure she would catch up to her husband and all would end well. His tracks were easy to follow.
One day, she found his hat. She put it on, and again, there was excrement inside it. She was getting disgusted. “Why are his clothes like this?” she wondered. She just carried the hat.

sentence.sent_text: Minwendam e-babimosed awe ikwe, aaniish naa ningoding igo ji-adimaad ini onaabeman.

paragraph.text_eng: It was now very warm. The sun shone warmly in the after-noons. She was getting warm too as she was walking. And she was still following her husband’s footprints. sentence.sent_text: Ishe, wiinge ngwana moowiwan iwe aanikwaan.

paragraph.text_eng: She kept on going. Soon she found a moccasin. It was filled with excrement. Awful! She didn’t say anything to herself. She just picked it up. Soon, she found the other moccasin. Sometimes, she would find a piece of excrement on the trail. She kept on walking. Finally she came to the end of his tracks. There on the bare ground—-because the snow had melted by now-—in all its glory was her own excrement that she had spo-ken to in the fall. It was the one that she had said she would marry if it were a man. That is what she had married. She went home in humility. When she got home, she agreed to marry whoever would have her and that’s what she did.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash eta go enendang, ndigo gii-ani-wawaaga'amiikawewan ini gaa-bima'anaad.

chapter.eng_title: The Women Who Married the Star Men

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago, there were two young women who decided to sleep out in the open. They didn’t sleep in a wiigiwaam that night. The sky was totally cloudless. Only the stars were visible everywhere they looked above them. They didn’t go to sleep right away, they were laughing and having a good time. They lay on their backs looking at the sky, gazing at the stars.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin dash zhemaak nibaasiiwag, wiinge nibaadaapiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: “Which star would you marry if you had to choose one?” asked one young woman to the other.
“I would pick that large one there.” She pointed at a very big bright star. “How about you?”

sentence.sent_text: "Iya'aa niin nin-daa-odaapinaa awe maawach gaa-man-gaanzhed," ikido awe ikwe, "giin dash wiin?"

paragraph.text_eng: “I would pick that one that’s a bit red,“ said the other young woman. After that, they got tired of looking at the sky and fell asleep.

sentence.sent_text: "Awe niin bangii gaa-miskwaanzhed nin-daa-wiidige-maa ," ikido awe miinawaa ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: When they woke up in the morning, they looked around. They were not in the same place where they were when they went to sleep the night before. They couldn’t see any trees around. It was just bare ground everywhere. There was no lake close by. It just looked very very different.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge sa go bakaan izhinaagwanini gaa-izhi-goshkoziwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: And they were also sleeping beside two strange men. One man was very thin and the other man was big and burly.

sentence.sent_text: Awe nitam ikwe zhiigwaakoziwan inini-wan gaa-wiipemaad.

paragraph.text_eng: The two women looked at each other. They realized where they were. They were up in the sky and those were stars that they were with.

And so they settled down to live there. They were mar-ried. The men that they married were very good to them. They treated the women kindly and the women had nothing to complain about. They were fed well, and their wiigiwaams were beautiful. They did their part in keeping them clean and organized.

sentence.sent_text: Amii sa imaa gaa-daawaad, aaniish inaa onaabemiwag noongom.

paragraph.text_eng: The women lived there for quite a while. But one day, they started to miss their own home back on earth. They were miss-ing their relatives that they had left behind.

sentence.sent_text: Ginwezhiish igo imaa gii-daawag igi ikwewag.

paragraph.text_eng: One day when they were wandering about on that Star Land, they saw an old woman sitting inside a little wiigiwaam.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash e-babaamosewaad imaa anangoowaki-ing , o-gii-waabamaawaan mindimooyen wiigiwaamensing e-namadabinid.

paragraph.text_eng: That old woman was fishing with a long string. “What are you fishing for?” they asked her. They went over to where she was. In the middle of her little wiigiwaam, there was a hole.

sentence.sent_text: Naawiya'ii dash imaa wiigiwaamensing, bagwanekamigaani ngwana.

paragraph.text_eng: The old woman was peering into that hole. Into that hole was where her long string was being dropped, that’s where she was fishing. They looked into that hole too.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa waasa gichi-giizhigong ayaawag, wenjii-waasawinaagwaninig aki.
Ningoding gii-waabamad migizi gii-gagiizhibaayaashid ishpiming, biinish dash gii-ani-angwaashid waasa ishpiming, amii iinzan ini mindimooyen gaa-gwaashkwebinigod.
Amii dash ge-doodamamban mookomaan ji-aabajitooyin, owe ji-doo-daman , "gi-bakizhon" dash ji-inad awe migizi.

paragraph.text_eng: They could see their home earth down below. It was very, very far away. They saw an eagle being caught by the old wom-an. Sometimes when you see an eagle circling and circling in the sky, it will soon keep flying higher and higher until it disap-pears. It is being caught by that old woman in the Star Country. And so you should take a knife and aim it at the sky and say, “I cut you free,” and the eagle will be released.

sentence.sent_text: Wiinge sa zhagadendamoog igi ikwewag, e-waaban-damowaad gaa-onjiiwaad.
O-ganoonaawaan ini mindi-mooyen , "ganage gi-daa-niisaabiiginishinaam ji-giiweyaang gaa-onjiiyaang.

paragraph.text_eng: The two women were very lonesome for their home when they saw where they came from. They asked the old woman, “please lower us down so we could go home to our own coun-try. We want to see our relatives again.”

sentence.sent_text: Gii-dibaajimowag gaye aaniin iinzan ezhised migizi gii-gagiizhibaayaashid ishpiming, ji-bakizhond ningoding, ji-manaa-bichizhond dash eta.

paragraph.text_eng: And they were pitied by the old woman. She agreed to low-er them down on that string. And that’s how the women were able to return home. They told about where they had gone. They told about what happens to eagles when they fly in cir-cles in the sky and how to cut them free, and to try not to cut an eagle accidentally. The women tried to do well in their lives here. They didn’t make mischief anymore.
Animals were able to talk to each other long ago, just like we use language to talk to each other today. That’s what animals did too.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-nitaa-gaagiigidowag aya'aawishag mewinzha, daabish-koo sa go anishinaabeg gaa-inwewaad gii-gaganoonidiwaad gii-ayizhiiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: One time, Wolf was talking to Fox. They were discussing who had the ability to stay awake longest, like all night. “I would be able to stay awake all night,” said Fox. “I could beat you in a contest,” he said to Wolf.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash iinzan Ma'iingan o-dazhi-gaganoonaan Waagoshan.
Odazhindaanaawaa iinzan awenen ge-gashki-toopan gabe-dibik ji-nibaasig.
"Niin nin-daa-gashkitoon iwe ji-doodamaan," iinzan ikido awe Waagosh, "gi-daa-bakina'on wii-gagwe-bakinaadiying," odinaan Ma'iinganan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Alright, let’s go into a contest,” said Wolf to the Fox.

sentence.sent_text: "Haaw sa, gagwe-aada'odidaa," odinaan Waagoshan awe Ma'iingan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so they began their contest. A bird was designated to monitor the two contestants, to make sure they stayed awake. In the evening, they began their contest. They built a fire out-side. And that’s where they sat all night. They were looking at each other. They talked to each other. And then they would go back to staring at each other. Soon it was the middle of the night. They were still awake. Then they started singing songs, hoping to lull each other to sleep. But that didn’t work.

Soon it looked like dawn was coming. They were both starting to get drowsy at last. Wolf really wanted to sleep. As he sat there, he’d fall forwards. Then he’d right himself imme-diately. Same with Fox. He would almost fall asleep too. Both of them were struggling to stay awake. Finally Fox put twigs in his eyes to prop his eyelids open; that’s how badly he wanted to stay awake.

sentence.sent_text: Gegapii awe Waagosh mitigoon-san gaa-izhi-aabajitood ji-baakiiga'ang oshkiinzhigoon e-biichi-wii-gashkanzagwaabisig.

paragraph.text_eng: In the morning, only Wolf was still sitting upright. Fox was laying there. He had fallen asleep and the twigs were sticking out of his eyes. That’s what he had done to keep his eyes open, but in vain.

sentence.sent_text: E-ani-waabang Ma'iingan eta giiyaabi gii-gwayak-waakobi imaa.
Waagosh wiin gii-bimishin, amii wiin e-gii-gawingoshid, mitigoonsan zaasaagaakosininiwan imaa oshkiinzhigoong, amii iinzan gaa-doodang e-gii-gagwe-doos-kaabaako'od izod.

paragraph.text_eng: This story is about a time when animals could talk to each oth-er. So one time, the dogs were living by themselves in their own village. They were enemies with the Cats. One day, the Dogs decided to have a meeting to discuss what to do about the Cats. They all walked in a large wiigiwaam in single file to hold their meeting there. It was their custom at that time, when they entered a wiigiwaam, to remove their bums and hang them by the door. The bums would hang there in a straight line. When they left, they would put them back on again. So they did that at this meeting. So they sat there at their meeting, sitting on the ground like usual. They were venting how they were feeling about those Cats.

sentence.sent_text: Aapiji iinzan gii-zhiingenindiwag igi Animoshag gaye Boozhi-insag.
Aabiding dash iinzan gii-maawaji'idiwag igiwe Animoshag e-wii-dazhimaawaad ini Boozhiinsa' ozaam e-ani-baatiinonid.
Amii dash iinzan ako gaa-izhichigewaad Ani-moshag gii-biindigewaad endaawaad gemaa aaniindi go, e-gii-giichigonaawaad ojiidiiwaa'.
Bazigwanjisewag gakina, imaa dash ishkwaandeng apa'idiwag, wewiib omanibinaawaan ojiidiimaan, e-ani-zaagijibatoowaad dash.
Apii agwajiing gii-niibawiwaad, o-gii-gikendaanaawaa anishaa iinzan e-gii-igowaad ini Boozhiinsan.
Amii sa gaaw-iin o-gii-gikendanziinaawaa awenenan ojiidiin gaa-bisika-waawaad.
Amii dash noongom wenji-mamiinaandiwaad Animoshag e-gagwe-mikawaawaad ojiidiiwaan.

paragraph.text_eng: And the Cats knew that this meeting was taking place. One cat snuck over to where the Dogs were meeting. He peered inside and yelled, “Fire! Oh no, there’s a fire! Run out!” All the Dogs sprang to their feet in panic and ran to the door. In their hurry to get out of the wiigiwaam, they grabbed any bum they could grab and ran outside. Once they got outside, they had forever mixed up their bums. Still to this day, each Dog will go around and sniff another Dog’s bum, wondering if that belongs to him.

Long ago there lived a man. Apparently he was very vain. He thought so highly of himself. He thought he was the handsom-est man of all. And everywhere he looked, when he saw beauty, he thought it was because of him. He also liked looking at his penis, studying it closely and talking to it.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding iinzan ayaagoban inini, aapiji iinzan gii-ishpen-indizo awe inini.
Amii iinzan ako gaye endoodang ewaabamidizod miziwe e-onizhishinang gaa-waabandang.
Ojoow iinzan ako gaye o-gii-nitaa-waawaabandaan, egaganoodang gaye.

paragraph.text_eng: Then one time, he was walking along in the middle of a fro-zen lake. He saw a herd of caribou walking on the ice. He asked his penis, “Do you see those caribou walking on the ice?” The penis didn’t say anything. He asked again, “Do you see them walking?” Finally, in exasperation, the penis answered him.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash iinzan mishawakom ebimaadagaakod, owaabamaa' adikwa' ebimaadagaakonid.
Oganoodaan iinzan owiinag, "Gi-waabamaag na igi gaa-bimaad-agaakowaad?"

paragraph.text_eng: “I see them!” is what it said. “I see them!” in a loud voice. And then again, “I see them!” That’s all it said. And it kept say-ing the same thing over and over. It wouldn’t shut up. Because the caribou could hear the loud voice of the penis talking, they took fright and ran off. There went his meal. The penis kept talking, “I see them! I see them! I see them! I see them!” The man tried to close the mouth of the penis but it kept talking, “I see them!”

sentence.sent_text: Amii gaa-izhi-ozhimowaad igi adikwag enoondamowaad iwe e-giigidoomaganinig.
Amii sa apane igi adikwag gaa-animibatoowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: He went home. He asked his wife to try to help him shut up the penis. She couldn’t do it. The penis kept on talking, “I see them! I see them! I see them! I see them!” Finally it was his mother-in-law who was able to close the mouth of her son-in-law’s penis and cause it to stop talking.

sentence.sent_text: Owiiwan iinzan o-daana-gag-we-wiiji'goon , e-gagwe-gibodoonenang iweni wiinag.
Wiin awe o-gii-gashkitoon ji-gibodoonenang iweni wiinag.

paragraph.text_eng: This happened long ago before the white man came to the Thunder Bay area. The native people used to go to the Thun-der Bay area. These were native people who spoke other languages, not just those who spoke Ojibwe. They came from everywhere—-from the west, from the north, from the east and from the south. These would have included the Dakotah peo-ple from the south.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha jibwaa-dagoshinoowaad wemitigoozhiwag omaa gidakiinaang, gii-nitaa-izhaawag iinzan ako anishinaabeg imaa Animikii-wiikwedong.
Gaawiin wiin eta go gaa-in-weying gaa-inwewaad anishinaabeg.
Miziwe go gii-bi-on-jiiwag , ningaabii'anong, giiwedinong, waabanong, gaye zhaawanong, Bwaanag maawiin gewiinawaa zhaawanong inake gii-bi-onjiiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: They came to gather medicine that grew on top of Thun-der Bird Mountain. This medicine does not grow anywhere else but on top of that mountain. And so that’s why people came from all over, to gather this medicine. And they all respected each other when they saw each other.

sentence.sent_text: Mashkiki dash gaa-gii-bi-naanzikamowaad enitaawigig ogidajiw imaa Animiikii-wajiwing.
Gaawiin ningoji bakaan omaa nitaawigizinoodog iwe mashkiki gaa-gii-nitaawigig imaa ogidajiw.
Amii dash miziwe gaa-gii-bi-onjiiwaad anishinaabeg e-bi-moonzhaginamowaad iwe mashkiki-ini.

paragraph.text_eng: The Thunder Birds looked after this medicine. People would wait for a completely cloudless day before they would venture to climb the mountain. That would mean that the Thunder Birds were away hunting.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash iwe mashkiki gii-nitaawigig ogidajiw, bine-siwag , animikiig o-gii-ganawendaanaawaa.
Amii wedi ogidajiw gaa-danakiiwaad igi animikiig.

paragraph.text_eng: So one time, a small band of Ojibwes travelled from Lac Seul to go there to pick medicine. It must have taken them some time, maybe a few weeks to travel down there as they were paddling by canoe. They took great care to prepare for such a long trip. They finally got there and they made a camp where they would rest before climbing the mountain. They saw other people camped for the same reason. They too had to wait for a cloudless day to go up.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding dash omaa Obizhigokaang gii-onjiiwag anish-inaabeg wedi gewiinawaa gaa-izhaawaad Animikii-wiik-wedong.
Weweni gii-ozhiitaawag igi anishinaabeg ji-gashkitoowaad ji-dagoshinowaad wedi eminookamig gemaa e-niibing.
Namanch naa daso-dibik gaa-bimishkaawaa-wewag ji-dagoshinowaad wedi.
Apii dash gaa-dagoshinowaad wedi, o-gii-ozhitoonaawaa ge-izhi-gabeshiwaad ajina.
Baamaa aaniish wiinge go mizhakwak gii-akwaamajiwewag.
Giishpin biidaanakwag, amii igi binesiwag, animikiig imaa eyaawaad okwiin (aanakwa-dong).

paragraph.text_eng: So one day, they woke up to a cloudless day. That’s when they went up that mountain as quickly as they could. They only had so much time before a small cloud could form in the ho-rizon. The older men cautioned the young men not to touch the baby Thunder Birds they would see in the nests. They were given strict instructions not to bother them.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-waawiin-damawaawag igi oshkiniigiwag ji-manaa-zaaminaawaad ini binesiinsa' (animikiinsa')ge-waabamaawaad imaa waza-soning.

paragraph.text_eng: So they went up the mountain. They walked quickly. They had to go gather the medicine before a cloud formed.

sentence.sent_text: Wewiib aaniish ji-gagwe-dagoshinoowaad wedi, wewiib ji-moonzhaginamowaad mashkikiini jibwaa-biidaanakwag.

paragraph.text_eng: When they arrived up there, sure enough, they saw med-icine growing everywhere on top of that mountain. And they saw huge nests here and there. And in each nest sat a big baby Thunder Bird, flashing small lightning bolts out of its eyes as it looked around. They looked very amazing.

sentence.sent_text: Apii wedi gii-dagoshinowaad, debwe owaabandaa-naawaa mashkiki enitaawigig miziwe imaa ogidajiw.

paragraph.text_eng: When they had finished gathering their medicine, they got ready to make their way down, quickly again. Now there was one man, there is always one man, who was foolish and obsti-nate. He decided he would see what happened if he gave a little poke with a twig at one of the baby Thunder Birds. He did so and immediately there was a huge flash of lightning and clap of thunder. Then he was gone, burned to a crisp, like he had been struck by lightning. The other men took flight down the moun-tain, leaving their dead companion behind. They barely made it back to their camp when a terrible thunder storm struck. They were all safe in their wiigiwaams though. They were lucky. That is what happened one time long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Amii dash gii-ishkwaa-moonzhaginamowaad mash-kikiini , gii-ozhiitaawaad miinawaa ji-bi-niisaamajiwewaad, wewiib.
Bezhig dash inini gaa-gagiibaadizid dinookaan, gaa-zhazhiibitang, gii-inendam iinzan ji-dookinaad bezhig binesiinsan, mitigoons e-aabajitood.
Apane iinzan gaa-gichi-initaagwak, daabishkoo e-baaginaazod awiya.
Gii-gizhiiba'iwewag igi anishinaabeg, wedi dash ezhi-gabeshiwaad gii-dagoshinoog.
Gaawiin dash wiin gegoon gii-izhisesiiwag wiinawaa.
